title: Storage and indexes
summary: Match the store to the access path; say what an index costs on writes.

parts.rule: Pick storage from the access path: relational rows for rich queries and transactions, document or key-value for simple PK gets, wide-column for huge time-series keyed partitions, object storage for large blobs. An index is a second structure maintained on every write. State which queries the index accelerates and what insert latency you trade.
parts.why: Wrong store choice forces painful migrations. Over-indexing slows writes while under-indexing forces table scans at peak. Interviewers listen for the write tax when you propose a new secondary index.
parts.example: Links table keyed by code needs no secondary index for redirects. Adding list-by-owner means either INDEX(owner_id) on links or a separate owner_links table. Photo bytes go to object storage keyed by content hash; the database stores only the hash and metadata so a five megabyte upload does not bloat the transactional store. Time-series metrics with key (device_id, ts) fit a wide-column or time-series store better than a generic heap table scanned by device. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool. parts.use: Choose storage after the data model paths exist. Add indexes only for queries you already named. Put large opaque payloads in object storage with a pointer in the system of record.
parts.refuse: Refuse a new index for a query that runs once a day. Refuse storing multi-megabyte blobs in the OLTP row store. Refuse claiming "the database will figure it out" without an access path. Refuse five specialized stores on day one when one primary fits.

body:
Rule. Pick storage from the access path: relational rows for rich queries and transactions, document or key-value for simple PK gets, wide-column for huge time-series keyed partitions, object storage for large blobs. An index is a second structure maintained on every write. State which queries the index accelerates and what insert latency you trade.

Why it matters. Wrong store choice forces painful migrations. Over-indexing slows writes while under-indexing forces table scans at peak. Interviewers listen for the write tax when you propose a new secondary index.

Worked example. Links table keyed by code needs no secondary index for redirects. Adding list-by-owner means either INDEX(owner_id) on links or a separate owner_links table. With 100_000_000 rows, each insert now updates the secondary structure — fine at tens of writes per second, painful at tens of thousands without batching. Photo bytes go to object storage keyed by content hash; the database stores only the hash and metadata so a five megabyte upload does not bloat the transactional store. Time-series metrics with key (device_id, ts) fit a wide-column or time-series store better than a generic heap table scanned by device. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool. Hold the method and the cost in mind before naming a tool.

[[diagram:index]]

When to use. Choose storage after the data model paths exist. Add indexes only for queries you already named. Put large opaque payloads in object storage with a pointer in the system of record.

When to refuse. Refuse a new index for a query that runs once a day. Refuse storing multi-megabyte blobs in the OLTP row store. Refuse claiming "the database will figure it out" without an access path. Refuse five specialized stores on day one when one primary fits.
